headline: Consumer prices rose 0.4 percent in August and 3.4 percent over 12 months; real hourly earnings fell 0.1 percent

items.title: Consumer Price Index, August 2026
items.summary: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers rose 0.4 percent in August on a seasonally adjusted basis, and 3.4 percent over the twelve months ending in August before seasonal adjustment. Leaving out food and energy, the index rose 0.3 percent in the month and 2.4 percent over the year. The energy index rose 2.1 percent in August and 16.3 percent over twelve months; the food index rose 0.1 percent; shelter rose 0.3 percent in the month and 3.0 percent over the year.
items.meaning: The CPI measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services; this figure is for all urban consumers. A 3.4 percent yearly rise means a basket that cost $100 a year earlier cost about $103.40 in August. Most of the gap between the all-items figure and the figure excluding food and energy is energy.

items.title: Real Earnings, August 2026
items.summary: Real average hourly earnings for all employees fell 0.1 percent from July to August, seasonally adjusted, as average hourly earnings rose 0.3 percent and the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers rose 0.4 percent. From August 2025 to August 2026, real average hourly earnings fell 0.3 percent, seasonally adjusted. Real average weekly earnings rose 0.2 percent over the month, with the average workweek up 0.3 percent, and were 0.3 percent higher over the year.
items.meaning: Real earnings are average earnings adjusted for changes in consumer prices, so they show what pay can buy rather than the dollar amount. A 0.1 percent decline in real hourly earnings means average hourly pay rose in dollars in August but by less than consumer prices did.

items.title: Monthly Treasury Statement, August 2026
items.summary: The Monthly Treasury Statement showed federal receipts of $360.0 billion and outlays of $526.8 billion in August 2026, a deficit of $166.8 billion. For fiscal year 2026 through August 31, receipts totaled $4,845.5 billion and outlays $6,811.0 billion, a deficit of $1,965.6 billion, compared with $1,973.3 billion in the same period of fiscal year 2025. Treasury notes that several payments normally made on August 1, including outlays for military active duty and retirement, veterans benefits, and Supplemental Security Income, were made in July because August 1, 2026 fell on a non-business day, while veterans benefit payments due September 1, 2026 were made in August.
items.meaning: The deficit is the amount by which outlays exceed receipts over a period. Single months are sensitive to calendar effects such as payment dates, which is why Treasury flags them; Treasury also notes that August has been a deficit month in 71 of 72 fiscal years because no major tax payments fall due in August.

items.title: Business Formation Statistics, August 2026
items.summary: The Census Bureau reported 531,728 business applications in August 2026, adjusted for seasonal variation, 7.8 percent fewer than in July 2026. Projected business formations within four quarters for August applications, also seasonally adjusted, were 28,501, down 4.6 percent from the July projection.
items.meaning: Applications and formations are different measures. The projected formations figure is the Census Bureau's estimate of how many businesses with payroll tax liabilities will come from the month's applications within four quarters of applying; it is not a count of businesses that started in August.

sections.title: One concept to know
sections.text: Headline inflation is the change in the whole CPI basket. Core inflation leaves out food and energy, whose prices swing with harvests and oil markets. Neither is more real than the other: households pay headline prices, but core is a steadier read on the underlying trend. In August the two differed by a full percentage point over the year — 3.4 percent against 2.4 percent — and energy accounted for most of the gap.
